# Anumāna Sutta (MN 15 (PTS MN i 95))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Anumāna Sutta* (MN 15) is a discourse delivered by the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, classifying it within the commentarial category of the "words of disciples" (*sāvakabhāsita*) alongside texts such as the *Anaṅgaṇa* and *Sammādiṭṭhi* suttas [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Bapat & Hirakawa 1970]. Addressed to fellow monks, the discourse focuses on the necessity of mutual admonishment for communal well-being and lists the specific qualities that render a monastic difficult to admonish (*dubbacajātika*) or easy to admonish (*subbacajātika*) [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Horner]. Moggallāna instructs monks to undertake rigorous self-examination (*attanā va attānam paccavekkhitabbaṁ*), employing the simile of a person inspecting their reflection in a clean mirror to detect and voluntarily remove unwholesome mental states through the conative energy (*viriya*) of discernment (*paññā*) [Devdas 2004].

Owing to its strong focus on monastic discipline and self-correction, the commentary records that the ancient authorities (*porāṇā*) designated the sutta as the *Bhikkhupātimokkha* [Adikaram 1946]. It was traditionally recommended for daily reflection and integrated into monastic study curricula alongside the *Pātimokkha*, the *Khuddasikkhā*, and the *Dasadhamma Sutta* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; French & Nathan 2014]. Its analysis of the monk who is difficult to admonish directly parallels the Vinaya definition of *dubbacajātika* under the twelfth *saṅghādisesa* rule [Horner].

Full parallels are preserved in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 89), an individual Chinese translation (T 50), and Śamathadeva's Tibetan *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* (Up 4.081). DharmaNexus aligns the text with passages in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (ZH_T01_0026) and Sanskrit and Tibetan Prātimokṣa literature [DharmaNexus]. Internally, DharmaNexus identifies 3,476 shared text-reuse segments across 64 Pali works, with extensive parallels in the *Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta* (MN 151), various sections of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10, AN 6, AN 8, AN 3, AN 4), the *Dīgha Nikāya* compendia (DN 33, DN 34), and Vinaya procedural texts [DharmaNexus].
